cards.question: Why is applying the address-of operator & to a variable declared with register a compile-time error in C?
cards.answer: CPU registers do not have memory addresses in RAM, and the ISO C standard strictly forbids taking the address of any register variable regardless of whether the compiler places it in a register or on the stack.

cards.question: Can a global (file-scope) variable in C be declared with the register storage class?
cards.answer: No. The register specifier can only be applied to local variables (block scope) and function parameters; it cannot be applied at file scope.

cards.question: Can individual members of a struct be declared with the register storage class in C?
cards.answer: No. The register modifier can be applied to an entire struct variable, but cannot be applied to individual struct members.

cards.question: Is it valid to declare a pointer variable with register and assign it the address of a standard variable (e.g. register int *ptr = &val;)?
cards.answer: Yes. The pointer variable itself is stored in a CPU register, while the memory address it holds points to valid RAM.
